segments.translit: śabarapādo hi siddhācāryyastamevārthaṃ mahākaruṇārasaviddho lokārthāya pratipādayati—
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Śabarapāda]{p-sabara}, pierced by the flavour of great [compassion]{karuna}, sets forth that same meaning for the good of the world:
segments.note: Munidatta presents the song as the siddha master [Śabarapāda]{p-sabara}, pierced by the flavour of great [compassion]{karuna}, setting out 'that same meaning' once more, for the good of the world (cp.28.m1).

flags.note: Attribution. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song with Saraha's name (bar Di zhes pa'i glu dbyangs sa ra ha'i zhabs kyi'o), but its version of this opening comment agrees with the Sanskrit in naming the siddha master sa wa ri pa (grub pa'i slob dpon sa wa ri pa'i zhabs kyis) (cp.28.m1). At cp.28.m7 the Tibetan again has Saraha (sa ra ha'i zhabs bdag gis) where the Sanskrit has Śabarapāda. The attribution is kept as Śabarapāda, following the Sanskrit and the song's own self-naming (the mad Śabara of 7a).

The emphatic particle hi is left untranslated (cp.28.m1). 'That same meaning' (tam evārtham) presumably points back to the teaching of the earlier songs; the Tibetan has don de nyid, 'that very meaning'.

segments.translit: um̐cetyādi| yogīndrasya svakāyakaṅkāladaṇḍamunnataṃ sumeruśikharāgre mahāsukhacakre| sakāraparo hakāraḥ sa eva pavidharaḥ| tasya gṛhiṇī jñānamudrā nairātmā am̐kārajā vasati| mayūrāṅgamiti| nānāvicitra [42ka] pakṣavikalparūpaṃ svarūpeṇādhivāsyatayā paridhānamalaṅkāraṃ kṛtaṃ| guñje(ñja)ti grīvāyāṃ sambhogacakre guhyamantramāvike'pi vidhṛtā| padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyaṃ|
segments.translation: 'High…' and so on. The [stick]{danda} of the skeleton of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}'s own [body]{body}, raised high; at the tip of the peak of [Sumeru]{pl-sumeru}, in the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. The letter ha that comes after the letter sa: he is the [vajra]{vajra}-holder. His [wife]{grhini}, the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, born of the syllable aṃ, dwells there. 'Peacock feathers' (mayūrāṅga): the many and various forms of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about [sides]{paksa}, as they are made to rest in their [true nature]{svarupa}, are made her garment, her [ornament]{alankara}. 'Guñjā': at the [neck]{kantha}, the [wheel of enjoyment]{sambhoga-cakra}, she wears the secret [mantra]{mantra} too. The [refrain]{dhruvapada} is to be understood with the [verse]{pada} that follows the [verse]{pada}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the mountain as the raised 'stick' of the yogi's skeleton, and 'there' as Sumeru's summit, the wheel of great bliss; the Śabarī there is [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, the vajra-holder's wife. Her peacock feathers are conceptual thoughts, worn as dress; her garland, secret mantra at the throat. His last sentence points to the following verse, couplet 2, as the refrain (cp.28.m2).

equations.en: the raised stick of the skeleton of the lord of yogis' own body
at the tip of Sumeru's peak, in the wheel of great bliss
the vajra-holder's wife, the jñānamudrā Nairātmā, born of the syllable aṃ
the many and various forms of conceptual thought about sides, made her garment and ornament
the secret mantra, worn at the neck
the wheel of enjoyment

flags.note: The refrain sentence, padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyam (cp.28.m2), is rendered literally: 'The refrain is to be understood with the verse that follows the verse.' Coming at the end of his comment on couplet 1, it is read as pointing to the verse that follows this one, couplet 2, as the refrain, and the unit marks couplet 2 (2a, 2b) as the refrain on this basis. The Tibetan, rkang pa gzhan gyi rkang pas d+hU'i rkang par shes par bya'o, 'by the other foot (rkang pa) it is to be known as the dhru foot', takes uttara as 'other' (gzhan) and fits this reading; and the last couplet echoes 2a (umata sabaro, 7a). The alternative is to take uttarapada as 'the latter line' of this first verse, which would make 1b the refrain; Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b would suit that reading. His numbering: couplet 2 is his 'second verse' (cp.28.m3), his comment on couplet 3 has no number (cp.28.m4), and couplets 4–7 are his third to sixth (cp.28.m5–cp.28.m8). With couplet 2 as the refrain, left out of the count, couplets 4–7 come out right (couplet 1 first, couplet 3 second). The one oddity is that the 'second verse' heading stands on the refrain itself, while couplet 3, which should then be his second, is unnumbered.

sakāraparo hakāraḥ sa eva pavidharaḥ (cp.28.m2): translated 'the letter ha that comes after the letter sa', following the Tibetan sa yig gi pha rol ha yig, 'the letter ha beyond the letter sa'. In grammatical usage X-para can also mean 'followed by X', which would give 'ha followed by sa'. The point of the letter play is not explained. pavidhara is literally 'holder of the thunderbolt (pavi)', i.e. vajra-holder. The Tibetan reads the clause differently: 'the one who holds that very letter ha is the Śabara' (de nyid 'dzin pa de nyid sa wa ri'o), naming the Śabara where the Sanskrit has the vajra-holder, and with no word for pavi.

guhyamantramāvike'pi vidhṛtā (cp.28.m2) is corrupt: āvika means 'woollen' and makes no sense here, and it is left untranslated. My conjecture: read guhyamantramālikām api, 'she also wears the garland of secret mantra', which would answer the song's guñjā garland (মালী). The Tibetan has gu h+ya'i gsang sngags lhag par rnam par 'dzin pa, 'especially holds the secret mantra of guhya', with lhag par perhaps for adhi or api and no word for a garland. Shastri's guñje(ñja)ti is read as guñjeti, 'Guñjā'; the Tibetan glosses ma ru as guny+dza.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads this passage differently in three places (cp.28.m2). (1) For the skeleton (kaṅkāla) it has the spine (sgal tshigs kyi dbyig pa, 'staff of the spine'). (2) For tasya gṛhiṇī … vasati, 'his wife … dwells there', it has de'i khyim … la 'dug par byed do, 'he dwells in his house, the jñānamudrā Nairātmā', taking khyim, 'house', for gṛhiṇī and making the jñānamudrā the place where he lives; it also has a yig las skyes pa, 'born of the letter a', for am̐kārajā. (3) For pakṣavikalparūpaṃ svarūpeṇādhivāsyatayā it has phyogs kyi rnam par rtog pa'i gzugs kyis lhag par gnas pa, 'abiding by the form of conceptual thought about sides', with no word for svarūpa, 'true nature', as if reading -rūpeṇa once.

svarūpeṇādhivāsyatayā (cp.28.m2): adhivāsya (from adhi-vas, causative) can mean 'to be perfumed or consecrated' as well as 'to be made to dwell'. I chose 'as they are made to rest in their true nature', which suits the Tibetan lhag par gnas pa, 'abiding'; 'as they are to be consecrated in their true nature' is possible. pakṣa means both 'wing, feather' and 'side', so the gloss seems to play on the peacock's feathers.

nānāvicitra in cp.28.m2 is the ordinary adjective 'many and various', not vicitra, the first of the four moments, so it is not marked with the glossary term (the automatic glossary hit is a false match). daṇḍa in kaṅkāladaṇḍa is marked with the glossary's 'stick'; 'staff' would read better in English and matches the Tibetan dbyig pa.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasvarūpamāha—
umata ityādi| bhagavatī nairātmyā bhāvakāyāśvāsaṃ dadāti| bho unmatta viṣayavihvalacitta śabara prājñopāyamelake| gulīti| ānandādivikalpaṃ mā kuru| ahaṃ tava gṛhiṇī jñānamudrā sahajasundarīti|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [practice]{abhyasa}:
'Mad…' and so on. The [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati} [Nairātmā]{nairatma} gives comfort to the [body]{body} of existence: 'O [mad]{unmatta} [Śabara]{sabara}, your [mind]{citta} overwhelmed by [sense objects]{visaya}, in the [union]{mela} of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}' — 'gulī' — 'do not form [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa} such as [joy]{ananda}. I am your [wife]{grhini}, the [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}, [Innate Beauty]{sahaja-sundari}.'
segments.note: Munidatta hears couplet 2 as the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma} comforting the Śabara, whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects: in the union of wisdom and means he must not form conceptual thoughts such as joy, which is how he explains 'do not make gulī'; she herself is his wife, the jñānamudrā, Innate Beauty (cp.28.m3). He leaves guhāḍā unexplained.

equations.en: whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects

equations.src: mā kara gulī (do not make gulī)
equations.en: do not form conceptual thoughts such as joy
the jñānamudrā, Nairātmā speaking of herself

flags.note: bhāvakāyāśvāsaṃ dadāti (cp.28.m3) is obscure. Taken as one compound, as Shastri prints it, it means 'gives comfort to the body of existence', perhaps the embodied yogin still caught in existence; that is the rendering chosen. Divided bhāvakāyā āśvāsaṃ, it would describe Nairātmā: 'she, whose body is being (or: in bodily form), gives comfort'. The Tibetan, bdag med ma'i ngo bos dbugs 'byin pa ster bar byed do, 'gives comfort through her nature as Nairātmā', reads bhāva as ngo bo, 'nature', and has no word for body.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of cp.28.m3 ends the address with sa wa ri thabs dang shes rab gcig pa'o, which reads as a statement, '(the) Śabara is the oneness of means and wisdom', where the Sanskrit's locative prājñopāyamelake, 'in the union of wisdom and means', gives the setting of the warning. It has 'khrul pa, 'deluded', for vihvala, 'overwhelmed'. In the last sentence it divides the name: ye shes kyi phyag rgya lhan cig skyes pa ni mdzes pa can no, 'the jñānamudrā; the innate one is the beautiful one'.
prājñopāya- (cp.28.m3) stands for the usual prajñopāya-, 'wisdom and means'. The goddess is spelled nairātmyā here (nairātmā elsewhere in this comment); both are rendered Nairātmā.

segments.translit: nānyetyādi| asya kāyasumeroḥ| taruvaraṃ avidyārūpaṃ| ānandādimantreṇa nānāprakāreṇa mukulitanijarūpaṃ gataṃ| anya ḍālañca pañcaskandhaṃ gagane prabhāsvare lagnaṃ| ataeva sā nairātmā ekakā| karṇeti, nānāsthāne kuṇḍalādipañcamudrāniraṃśukālaṅkāraṃ kṛtvā vajramupāyajñānaṃ vidhṛtya yuganaddharūpeṇa atra kāyaparvvatavane| hiṇḍati krīḍati|
segments.translation: 'Various…' and so on. Of this [body]{body}-[Sumeru]{pl-sumeru}: the [fine tree]{taruvara} has the form of [ignorance]{avidya}; through the [mantra]{mantra} of [joy]{ananda} and the rest, in various ways, it has come into bud in its own form. And its [branch]{branch}, the five [aggregates]{skandha}, touches the [sky]{gagana}, the [clear light]{prabhasvara}. That is why that [Nairātmā]{nairatma} is alone. 'Earrings…': having put on the [five seals]{pancamudra}, beginning with [earrings]{kundala}, at their various places, as the [ornament]{alankara} of one who wears no clothes, and holding the [vajra]{vajra}, the [knowledge]{jnana} of [means]{upaya}, in the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, here in the [forest]{forest} of the [body]{body}-[mountain]{mountain} — 'roams' means she [plays]{lila}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the budding trees as ignorance come into its own form through the mantra of the joys, and their branches touching the sky as the five aggregates touching clear light; so [Nairātmā]{nairatma} is alone. Unclothed, she wears the five seals, beginning with earrings; her vajra is the knowledge of means; the forest is the body-mountain, where she plays (cp.28.m4).

equations.en: ignorance (avidyārūpa)
the five aggregates
clear light
that Nairātmā, alone
the knowledge of means
the forest of the body-mountain
plays (krīḍati)

flags.note: Two slips in the printed text of cp.28.m4, corrected with the Tibetan: the headword nānyetyādi is read nānetyādi, 'Various… and so on' (Tibetan sna tshogs zhes bya ba la sogs pa, and the song's ṇāṇā); and anya ḍālañca is read asya ḍālañca, 'and its branch' (Tibetan 'di'i yal ga).

niraṃśuka in kuṇḍalādipañcamudrāniraṃśukālaṅkāraṃ (cp.28.m4) is taken as 'without clothing' (aṃśuka, 'garment'): the five seals are the ornament of one who wears nothing else. The glossary's automatic hit on niravayava, 'partless' (as if niraṃśa), is a false match. The Tibetan has instead phyag rgya lnga rus pa'i rgyan gyis brgyan par byas nas, 'adorned with the five seals, bone ornaments', with nothing for 'without clothing'.

Smaller differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of cp.28.m4: it has rgyas pa, 'flourishing, spread', for mukulita, 'in bud'; it begins the five seals with 'khor lo, 'wheel, ring', its word for kuṇḍala in the song line too (rna rgyan 'khor lo); and it has lus kyi ri bo, 'the body-mountain', with no word for forest (vana).

Munidatta gives this comment no verse number (cp.28.m4), although he calls couplet 2 his 'second verse' (cp.28.m3) and couplet 4 his 'third' (cp.28.m5). With couplet 2 as the refrain, couplet 3 would be his second verse. See the refrain flag on cp.28.m2.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena krīḍāsu[43]khaprav[āha]māha—
tia dhā ityādi| traidhātukaṃ kāyavākcittaṃ sukhaprabhāsvare taṃ ṭālayitvā tena mahāsukhena śayyāṃ kṛtvā śabaracittavajrabhuja(ca)ṅgena saha| dāriketi| kleśān dārayatīti dārikā nairātmā dārikā y[ā]| premamiti krīḍārasamanupamaṃ varddhayitvā rajanī| andhakāraṃ prajñopāyavikalpaṃ nāśitaṃ|
tathāca sarahapādāḥ—
śrīvajrāmṛta ityapi bhramayītyādi|
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the flow of the [bliss]{sukha} of [play]{lila}:
'Three worlds…' and so on. The [three worlds]{trailokya} are [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}: having spread them out in the [clear light]{prabhasvara} of [bliss]{sukha}, and having made the [bed]{bed} with that [great bliss]{mahasukha}, together with the [lover]{bhujanga}, the [Śabara]{sabara}'s mind-[vajra]{vajra}. 'Courtesan' (dārikā): she is a dārikā because she tears apart (dārayati) the [afflictions]{klesa}; [Nairātmā]{nairatma} is the dārikā. 'Love': having made the incomparable flavour of [play]{lila} grow. 'Night': the [darkness]{andhakara}, the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, is destroyed.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'Glorious [vajra]{vajra}-[nectar]{amrta} too whirls…', and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the three worlds as body, speech and mind, spread out in the clear light of bliss to make a bed of great bliss with the lover, the Śabara's mind-vajra. [Nairātmā]{nairatma} is the courtesan who 'tears apart' the afflictions; love is the growing flavour of play; night, the darkness of conceptual thought about wisdom and means, destroyed (cp.28.m5).

equations.en: body, speech and mind
the Śabara's mind-vajra
Nairātmā, called dārikā because she tears apart (dārayati) the afflictions
the incomparable flavour of play, made to grow
the darkness of the conceptual thought of wisdom and means, which is destroyed

citations.quoted: śrīvajrāmṛta ityapi bhramayītyādi ('Glorious vajra-nectar too whirls…', and so on)
citations.work: a verse of Saraha (Sarahapāda), quoted only by its opening; not identified

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit of cp.28.m5 has sukhaprabhāsvare, 'in the clear light of bliss', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nam mkha' la 'od gsal ba, 'in the sky, the clear light', as if reading kha, 'sky', for sukha (or dividing the syllables differently). The translation follows the Sanskrit.

The framing word of cp.28.m5 is damaged: Shastri restores prav[āha], 'flow', in krīḍāsukhapravāham, 'the flow of the bliss of play'. The Tibetan has rol pa'i bde ba'i stobs, 'the power of the bliss of play', which would suit prabhāva (or bala) rather than pravāha. Since the letters are Shastri's restoration, prabhāva is a real possibility; compare the prabhāva that opens cp.28.m6.

ṭālayitvā (cp.28.m5) is a rare verb. I translated 'having spread them out', following the Tibetan brkyang nas, 'having stretched out', which suits the making of a bed. If it is the Prakrit ṭal-, 'move away', it would mean 'having removed (or withdrawn) them into the clear light of bliss'. The pronoun taṃ is masculine singular, though it refers back to the neuter traidhātukaṃ kāyavākcittaṃ.

In cp.28.m5 the Tibetan takes bhujaṅga as 'snake' (ltos 'gro, 'belly-crawler'), as in its song line (sbrul), not as 'lover'; and for śayyāṃ kṛtvā, 'having made the bed', it has nyal bar byas nas, 'having made (them) lie down'.

nairātmā dārikā y[ā] (cp.28.m5) ends with a relative pronoun ('who'), with its ā restored by Shastri, and no correlative; it is rendered as a plain statement, as the Tibetan does (bdag med ma gzugs 'tshong ma'o, 'Nairātmā is the courtesan'). Shastri's danda after rajanī is moved: the Tibetan confirms that 'Night' (mtshan mo zhes pa ni) begins the next gloss.

The Saraha quotation in cp.28.m5 is only an opening, and bhramayī is an unclear (perhaps Apabhraṃśa) form; 'whirls' follows the Tibetan, dpal gyi rdo rje bdud rtsi nyid kyang 'khor, 'the glorious vajra, nectar itself too, turns'. One could also read śrīvajrāmṛta ity api as naming a second source, 'and also the Śrī Vajrāmṛta' (a tantra of that name exists, from my memory), with bhramayi… as the quotation; the Tibetan takes the whole as Saraha's line.

segments.translit:
caturthena phalahetubhāvaṃ prabhāvaṃ pratipādayati—
hiem̐ ityādi| hṛdayaṃ prabhāsvaraṃ tāmbūlenādhimucya karpūraṃ yuganaddharūpeṇa phalahetusambandhena tamadhimucya| śūnyamiti saiva sarvvākāravaropetaśūnyatā nairātmajñānayoginī| k[e]ṇṭhati sambhogacakre vidhṛtya mahāsukhajñānaraśminā rajanīti| svakāyakleśatamaḥ svayaṃ nāśitaṃ|
tathāca sūtake|
phalena hetumāmudrya ityādi|
segments.translation:
With the fourth he sets forth the [power]{prabhava}, the relation of [fruit]{phala} and [cause]{hetu}:
'Heart…' and so on. Having [resolved]{adhimukti} on the [heart]{hrdaya}, the [clear light]{prabhasvara}, as the [betel]{betel}; and the [camphor]{camphor}: having [resolved]{adhimukti} on it in the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, through the relation of [fruit]{phala} and [cause]{hetu}. 'Emptiness': she is that very [emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects]{sarvakaravaropeta}, the [yoginī]{yogini} who is the [knowledge]{jnana} of [selflessness]{nairatmya}. 'At the neck': holding her in the [wheel of enjoyment]{sambhoga-cakra}, with the rays of the [knowledge]{jnana} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. 'Night': the darkness of the [afflictions]{klesa} of his own [body]{body} is destroyed by himself.
And so in the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}: 'Sealing the [cause]{hetu} with the [fruit]{phala}…', and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the heart taken as betel as clear light, and the camphor as coupled union, in the relation of fruit and cause. The emptiness at the Śabara's neck is [Nairātmā]{nairatma} as emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, held in the wheel of enjoyment; the passing night is the darkness of his body's afflictions, destroyed by himself (cp.28.m6).

equations.en: clear light, resolved upon as the betel
coupled union, in the relation of fruit and cause
she, Nairātmā: the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, the yoginī who is the knowledge of selflessness
the wheel of enjoyment
the darkness of the afflictions of one's own body

citations.quoted: phalena hetumāmudrya ityādi ('Sealing the cause with the fruit…', and so on)

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of cp.28.m6 opens with the wrong headword: rma bya'i mdongs zhes bya ba la sogs pa, 'Peacock plumes and so on', naming the peacock plumes of couplet 1, where the Sanskrit quotes couplet 5 (hiem̐ ityādi, 'Heart… and so on'). Its comment that follows is on couplet 5.

Other differences in the Tibetan of cp.28.m6: the framing sentence has rgyu dang 'bras bu'i ngo bo, 'the nature of cause and fruit', with nothing for prabhāva, 'power'; it has snying gi 'od gsal, 'the clear light of the heart', for hṛdayaṃ prabhāsvaraṃ, 'the heart, the clear light', and go la, 'areca nut', for tāmbūla, 'betel'; it renders svayaṃ nāśitaṃ, 'destroyed by himself', as rang nyams pa, 'fades of itself'; and it quotes the Sūtaka as rgyu dang 'bras bu rgyas gdab pa, 'sealing cause and fruit', not 'the cause with the fruit'.

nairātmajñānayoginī (cp.28.m6) is rendered 'the yoginī who is the knowledge of selflessness'. It could also be 'Nairātmā, the knowledge-yoginī'. The Tibetan, bdag med ma'i ye shes rnal 'byor mas, reads the goddess (bdag med ma) and, with the agentive -s, makes her the subject of the holding at the neck that follows.

In cp.28.m6 the printed tāmvūlenādhimucyakarpūraṃ is divided tāmbūlena adhimucya karpūraṃ. The headword k[e]ṇṭhati, with Shastri's restored vowel sign, is read kaṇṭheti, 'At the neck' (Tibetan mgul pa ni). The instrumental mahāsukhajñānaraśminā, 'with the rays of the knowledge of great bliss', stands before rajanīti; it is attached to the holding, as in the Tibetan, though it could go with the destruction of the darkness.

segments.translit:
pañcamapadena vajragurumāhātmyamāha—
guruvākyetyādi| sa[43ka]dguruvākyena dhanuḥ kṛtvā nijamanobodhicittena bāṇa(na)ṃ ca| ekarasaṃ bāṇamiti ubhayorekaṃ kṛtvā ekasvaranirghoṣeṇa tamabhyasyamānaḥ san tena nirvvāṇena mayā sabarapādena anādyavidyāvāsanādoṣo hi hataḥ|
segments.translation:
With the fifth [verse]{pada} he states the [greatness]{mahatmya} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}:
'The [guru]{guru}'s word…' and so on. Making the true [guru]{guru}'s word the [bow]{bow}, and one's own [mind]{citta}, [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, the [arrow]{arrow}; 'the [arrow]{arrow} of [one taste]{ekarasa}': making the two one, and practising it with the resounding of a single note, through that [nirvāṇa]{nirvana} I, [Śabarapāda]{p-sabara}, have slain the fault of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of beginningless [ignorance]{avidya}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 6, his fifth verse, as the greatness of the vajra guru: the true guru's word is the bow, one's own mind, bodhicitta, the arrow; the single arrow is 'the arrow of one taste', the two made one. Speaking as [Śabarapāda]{p-sabara}, he says that through that nirvāṇa the fault of beginningless ignorance's tendencies is slain (cp.28.m7).

equations.src: gurubāka puñcaā (the guru's word as bow)
equations.en: the true guru's word, made the bow
bodhicitta
the arrow of one taste: the two made one

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit of cp.28.m7 has mayā sabarapādena, 'by me, Śabarapāda', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sa ra ha'i zhabs bdag gis, 'by me, Sarahapāda', in line with its heading, which gives the song to Saraha. Its opening comment (cp.28.m1), however, names sa wa ri pa. The attribution is kept as Śabarapāda.

Munidatta's headword ekarasaṃ bāṇam, 'the arrow of one taste' (cp.28.m7), stands for the song's eke śarasandhānem̐, 'with the arrow fitted once'; eke śara and ekarasa share their letters, so the gloss may play on the sound. ekasvaranirghoṣeṇa, 'with the resounding of a single note', is unexplained: perhaps the twang of the string, perhaps a single recited sound. The Tibetan has dbyangs gcig nges par sgrogs pas, 'by proclaiming a single tone'.

In cp.28.m7 the print spells the poet's name with dental s (sabarapādena) where cp.28.m1 has śabarapāda; Shastri's bāṇa(na)ṃ is read bāṇaṃ, 'arrow'. tena nirvāṇena, 'through that nirvāṇa', is rendered literally; the Tibetan agrees (de yis mya ngan las 'das pas).

segments.translit:
ṣaṣṭhapadena cittasya yathābhūtaṃ svarūpamāha—
umata ityādi| sahajapānapramatto mama cittavajro hi sabaraḥ garuā roṣeṇeti jñānānandagandhena preritaḥ san mahāsukhacakranalinīvanoddeśena pracalitaḥ| tatra nimagne sati girivareti| uktārtho mayā siddhācāryyeṇa kathaṃ anveṣayitavyaḥ|
tathācāgamaḥ|
yānānāṃ nāsti vai niṣṭhā yāvat cittaṃ pravarttate|
citte tattve pravṛtte hi na yānaṃ na ca yāyinaḥ||28||
segments.translation:
With the sixth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [mind]{citta} as it really is:
'Mad…' and so on. [Drunk]{matta} on the drink of the [innate]{sahaja}, my mind-[vajra]{vajra} is the [Śabara]{sabara}. 'In great [rage]{rosa}': impelled by the scent of the [joy]{ananda} of [knowledge]{jnana}, he has set out toward the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. When he has sunk into it — 'the great [mountain]{mountain}…' — how am I, the [siddha]{siddha} master, to seek the one whose meaning has been told?
And so the [scripture]{agama}:
'There is no end to the vehicles as long as the [mind]{citta} is active; when the [mind]{citta} has entered on [reality]{tattva}, there is neither vehicle nor traveller.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the mad Śabara as the poet's own mind-vajra, drunk on the drink of the innate; his great rage is the push of the scent of the joy of knowledge, sending him toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss. Once he has sunk there, how can the siddha master seek him (cp.28.m8)?

equations.en: my mind-vajra, drunk on the drink of the innate
the poet's own mind-vajra
impelled by the scent of the joy of knowledge, set moving toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss

citations.quoted: yānānāṃ nāsti vai niṣṭhā yāvat cittaṃ pravarttate | citte tattve pravṛtte hi na yānaṃ na ca yāyinaḥ
citations.work: Laṅkāvatārasūtra (Munidatta says only 'scripture', āgama); there the third quarter reads citte tu vai parāvṛtte

flags.note: In cp.28.m8 the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has pad+ma bzhin du gyen du rab tu bskyod pa, 'moving upward like a lotus', where the Sanskrit has mahāsukhacakranalinīvanoddeśena pracalitaḥ, 'set out toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss': it seems to divide nalinīvana as nalinī iva, 'like a lotus', and to render uddeśena, 'toward', as 'upward'. It also has dag gi, 'of those (drunk)', for mama, 'my', and chang, 'beer', for pāna, 'drink'.

The verse quoted in cp.28.m8 reads citte tattve pravṛtte hi, 'when the mind has entered on reality'. The Tibetan has sems nyid log par gyur pa la, 'when mind itself has turned back', which matches the form I remember from the Laṅkāvatāra, citte tu vai parāvṛtte, 'when the mind is transformed'. Shastri's text may be corrupt here; the translation follows it. The closing ||28|| is the song number and is not translated.

uktārthaḥ (cp.28.m8) is taken as 'the one whose meaning has been told', the Śabara just explained as the mind-vajra, subject of 'is to be sought'. The Tibetan takes it as the object, gsungs pa'i don, 'the meaning that was spoken'.

proposals.definition: Greatness, majesty (māhātmya; Tibetan bdag nyid che ba): one of the framing words with which Munidatta introduces a couplet. He says Śabarapāda's fifth verse, couplet 6 of song 28, states the greatness of the vajra guru (cp.28.m7). Compare power (prabhāva) and praise (anuśaṃsā).
proposals.rationale: A recurring framing word: besides cp.28.m7 (vajragurumāhātmya), the glossary's entry for path (marga) lists vartma(tmā)māhātmyam āhuḥ, 'they state the greatness of the path', as a form. The glossary already has entries for the parallel framing words prabhāva and anuśaṃsā.

questions: Refrain of song 28: couplet 2 is marked as the refrain, reading Munidatta's 'The refrain is to be understood with the verse that follows the verse' (cp.28.m2) as pointing to the verse after couplet 1. The alternative, 'the latter line' of the first verse, would make 1b the refrain and would suit Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b. One oddity remains in his count: the 'second verse' heading stands on couplet 2, the refrain (cp.28.m3), while his comment on couplet 3, which should then be his second, has no number (cp.28.m4); couplets 4–7 are his third to sixth (cp.28.m5–cp.28.m8). Should the song's notes mention this?

cittavajra ('mind-vajra', cp.28.m5, cp.28.m8) is listed as a form of trivajra, whose English is 'three vajras' and cannot stand for one vajra. I wrote mind-[vajra]{vajra}. Should trivajra take variants such as 'vajra of mind' and 'mind-vajra', or should the vajra of mind get its own entry?

cp.28.m2: guhyamantramāvike'pi is corrupt. Do you accept the conjecture guhyamantramālikām api, 'the garland of secret mantra', or should the passage be left marked as corrupt with only 'she wears the secret mantra'?

cp.28.m3: bhāvakāyāśvāsaṃ dadāti. I chose 'gives comfort to the body of existence' (one compound, as printed); 'she, embodied, gives comfort' (bhāvakāyā āśvāsaṃ) is also possible. Which do you prefer?

cp.28.m8: I identified the scripture verse as the Laṅkāvatārasūtra verse from memory (marked confident). Please check the identification and whether Shastri's citte tattve pravṛtte should be noted as a corruption of citte tu vai parāvṛtte, which the Tibetan supports.

cp.28.m5: should the Saraha quotation be left as Saraha's line, as the Tibetan takes it, or could śrīvajrāmṛta name a second source (a Vajrāmṛta tantra)? And should Shastri's restored pravāha give way to prabhāva, which the Tibetan stobs suggests?

Glossary matching: the automatic hits on vicitra (nānāvicitra, cp.28.m2) and niravayava (niraṃśuka, cp.28.m4) are false matches; their match forms may need narrowing. Also, kaṅkāladaṇḍa (cp.28.m2) is marked with danda 'stick'; would you allow 'staff' as a variant?
